content: The Evelyn tables are a collection of four anatomical preparations mounted on wooden boards, recognized as the oldest anatomical preparations in Europe. These tables were acquired by John Evelyn in Padua in 1646 and were later donated by him to the Royal Society. Currently, they are owned by the Royal College of Surgeons and are displayed at the Hunterian Museum in London. Additionally, six similar tables, brought to London from Italy by John Finch, are held by the Royal College of Physicians. Each of the Evelyn tables represents a different anatomical system of the human body. The structures, including arteries, nerves, and veins, were meticulously dissected from human specimens and affixed to wooden boards made from pine planks. These boards were planed, glued together, and coated with several layers of varnish. The dimensions of the boards are approximately 9 meters in height, 77 centimeters in width, and 10 centimeters in thickness. The first table displays the spinal cord and nerves, the second shows the aorta and arterial system, the third illustrates the vagus and sympathetic nerves along with the veins of the lungs and liver, and the fourth demonstrates the distribution of the venous system. John Evelyn spent several years outside England during the 1640s, a period marked by the English Civil War. His diary notes a visit to Padua in March 1646, where he attended dissection lectures at the University of Padua and acquired the four tables for a reported price of 150 scudi. Three of the tables—those depicting arteries, nerves, and veins—were prepared by Giovanni Leoni d’Este, a dissector working under Johann Vesling, the Professor of Anatomy at Padua. These were originally created for Leoni’s personal use. The fourth table, which features the vagus nerves, lungs, and liver, was specifically prepared by Leoni at Evelyn’s request. Evelyn eventually returned to London, and his diary records the arrival of the tables in April 1649, after a journey that was delayed in Holland en route from Venice. In October 1667, Evelyn donated the tables to the nascent Royal Society, which displayed them in its museum, referred to as the repository, located in the west gallery of Gresham College on Bishopsgate from 1674. On January 21, 1701, William Cowper presented a paper on the tables of arteries and veins, which was later published in Philosophical Transactions. His accompanying drawings were engraved by Michael van der Gucht. After the Royal Society relocated to a new site in Crane Court, off Fleet Street, the tables were acquired by the British Museum in June 1781, reflecting the museum's rapid expansion. Subsequently, in 1809, the tables were purchased by the Royal College of Surgeons, where they remain to this day.
